abstract: In many marine invertebrates, metamorphosis rapidly converts swimming larvae into morphologically distinct benthic juveniles, yet how cells coordinate this body plan transformation is unclear. Here we describe the first hours of metamorphosis in the sponge Amphimedon queenslandica using live and static imaging and CM-DiI-based cell tracing. Larval epithelial cells that mediate swimming and detect algal settlement cues - ciliated columnar, flask, globular and pigment ring cells - appear poised to transform, with changes beginning within 15 minutes of settlement. These transformations commence adjacent to the algal substrate and progress in a basoapical direction, producing 2-4 deep epithelial circumferential infoldings within 30-45 minutes. In concert with each infolding, larval cell types undergo distinct combinations of localised ingression, egression, de- and transdifferentiation, cilia resorption and mucus secretion. For example, epithelial flask cells become amoeboid, ingress and adopt an archaeocyte-like morphology. These observations indicate that widespread metazoan cell behaviours are integrated into a fast, spatially coordinated remodelling of the sponge body plan, and may provide a framework for understanding how morphogenetic programs are executed in metamorphosis more broadly.
